title: Setup Instructions for Students
text:
Follow these steps to set up and publish your research website.


Before you begin, make sure you have the following:

A GitHub account (free at github.com)
GitHub Desktop installed on your computer
R and RStudio







Click the “Use this template” button.
Select Create a new repository.
Use the Owner dropdown menu to select your github user
Name the repository. This will be in your web address! Choose something professional like your name.
Click Create repository from template.
You should now have this newly created repository on your own GitHub.





On your computer: Make sure the GitHub Desktop is open.
On GitHub: In your own repository on GitHub, Click the “<> Code” button.
Select Open with GitHub Desktop.
Choose a local path for the placement of the directory (not a cloud service). For example: (/Users/YourUserame/GitHub/introR2026)
Select Clone.





[!IMPORTANT] 1. Open RStudio 2. Create a new Rproj file in the existing local directory of your repository 3. Open .Rproj file 4. Edit the following files in RStudio




Replace “Your Name” with your name.
Update the About Me section.
Add your research interests.
Replace “your photo.jpg” with the filename of a photo of yourself & by adding the photo to the directory.
Update places that say “link” with the correct internet link or email address, if desired.





Update the descriptions of your projects.
Add links to additional projects as you create them.





Change the title to your project title.
Write your final report.
Replace all placeholder text with your own content.




styles.css * Customize colors, fonts, and other styling options if desired.
_quarto.yml * add new links to the navbar
README.md * This is a place to add information to the GitHub reponsitory, but will not be displayed on your rendered website.
.gitignore * List files here you don’t want synced to GitHub. For example, if you want to keep your data.csv files local and not online list them here
SETUP.md * These are instructions to create this site. No need to modify this file.




In RStudio, you can preview your website before publishing.
Run the following command in the RStudio Terminal:
quarto preview
To render the website before pushing your changes, run:
quarto render



When you are satisfied with your changes:

Open GitHub Desktop.
Review the files you modified.
Enter a commit summary and an optional description.
Click Commit to main.
Click Push origin to upload your changes to GitHub.





Go to your repository on GitHub.
Click Settings.
Select Pages from the left sidebar.
Under Build and deployment:

Source: Select Deploy from a branch.
Branch: Select main.
Folder: Select /docs.

Click Save.





Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub to deploy your site.
Return to Settings → Pages.
You should see a URL similar to:
https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/YOUR-REPOSITORY/
Click the link to view your website.





Whenever you want to update your website:

Edit your .qmd files.
Commit and push your changes using GitHub Desktop.
Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub Pages to rebuild your site.
Refresh your browser to view the updated website.




If your website is not updating:

Go to your GitHub repository.
Click the Actions tab.
Open the most recent workflow run.
Review any error messages if the build failed.







Go to Settings → Pages.
Confirm that:

The branch is set to main.
The folder is set to /docs.

Your website URL should appear on this page after deployment.




Always use forward slashes (/) in links, even when using Windows.
# Correct
[Link](projects/final-report.qmd)

# Incorrect
[Link](projects\final-report.qmd)




To add another page, such as a poster, publication, or additional project:

Create a new .qmd file in the projects/ folder.
Edit projects.qmd and add a link to the new page.
Commit and push your changes.
Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub Pages to update your website.





Quarto Documentation
GitHub Pages Documentation
Markdown Guide
Git Basics


Need help? Contact your instructor or refer to the resources listed above.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Maternal health risk assessment is important for identifying pregnant women who may require additional medical care. In this project, I will analyze a maternal health risk dataset collected from hospitals and community clinics in rural Bangladesh. The dataset includes maternal age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, heart rate, and maternal risk level.
I will use R to compare low-, mid-, and high-risk groups, examine relationships among the clinical measurements, and determine whether principal component analysis can reveal patterns among the maternal risk categories.




library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(here)

here() starts at C:/2. Class/R/Final project/Brototi-Chakrabarty





The dataset will be imported and analyzed using R and the tidyverse package. I will examine the structure and quality of the data, summarize the clinical measurements, and create bar charts, boxplots, scatterplots, and correlation plots. Principal component analysis will also be used to explore whether the maternal risk categories show distinct patterns.




maternal_data <- read_csv(
  here("data", "Maternal Health Risk Data Set.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)





glimpse(maternal_data)

Rows: 1,014
Columns: 7
$ Age         <dbl> 25, 35, 29, 30, 35, 23, 23, 35, 32, 42, 23, 19, 25, 20, 48…
$ SystolicBP  <dbl> 130, 140, 90, 140, 120, 140, 130, 85, 120, 130, 90, 120, 1…
$ DiastolicBP <dbl> 80, 90, 70, 85, 60, 80, 70, 60, 90, 80, 60, 80, 89, 75, 80…
$ BS          <dbl> 15.00, 13.00, 8.00, 7.00, 6.10, 7.01, 7.01, 11.00, 6.90, 1…
$ BodyTemp    <dbl> 98, 98, 100, 98, 98, 98, 98, 102, 98, 98, 98, 98, 98, 100,…
$ HeartRate   <dbl> 86, 70, 80, 70, 76, 70, 78, 86, 70, 70, 76, 70, 77, 70, 88…
$ RiskLevel   <chr> "high risk", "high risk", "high risk", "high risk", "low r…






maternal_data <- maternal_data |>
  mutate(
    RiskLevel = str_to_lower(str_trim(RiskLevel)),
    RiskLevel = factor(
      RiskLevel,
      levels = c("low risk", "mid risk", "high risk"),
      ordered = TRUE))


levels(maternal_data$RiskLevel)

[1] "low risk"  "mid risk"  "high risk"







First, I will count the number of observations in each maternal risk category.

maternal_data |>
  count(RiskLevel, sort = TRUE) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = n,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n),
    vjust = -0.4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Observations in Each Maternal Risk Category",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Number of Observations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Low-risk observations were the most common, with 406 records (40.0%). Mid-risk observations included 336 records (33.1%), while high-risk observations included 272 records (26.8%). Although the high-risk group was the smallest category, it still represented more than one-quarter of the dataset.



Maternal age will be compared across the low-, mid-, and high-risk categories.

maternal_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = Age,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Maternal Age Across Risk Categories",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Age"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Maternal age differed across the three risk categories. The high-risk group had a higher median age than the low- and mid-risk groups, although the age distributions overlapped. This suggests that higher maternal age is associated with increased risk classification in this dataset.



Systolic and diastolic blood pressure will be compared among the three maternal risk categories.

maternal_data |>
  select(RiskLevel, SystolicBP, DiastolicBP) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(SystolicBP, DiastolicBP),
    names_to = "BloodPressureType",
    values_to = "BloodPressure"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = BloodPressure,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~BloodPressureType,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Blood Pressure Across Maternal Risk Categories",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Blood Pressure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Both systolic and diastolic blood pressure were higher in the high-risk group than in the low- and mid-risk groups. The median systolic blood pressure was approximately 130 mmHg in the high-risk group compared with about 120 mmHg in the other groups, while the median diastolic blood pressure was approximately 90 mmHg compared with about 75 mmHg. Although the distributions overlapped, the results suggest that higher blood pressure is associated with a higher maternal risk classification in this dataset.



Blood sugar measurements will be compared among the low-, mid-, and high-risk groups.

maternal_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = BS,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Blood Sugar Across Maternal Risk Categories",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Blood Sugar"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()












Share your findings here. You can include:

Text explanations
Tables
Figures and visualizations
Code examples (if relevant)



Here’s a sample R code block:

library(ggplot2)

# Create some sample data
data <- data.frame(
  x = 1:10,
  y = rnorm(10)
)

# Make a plot
plot(data$x, data$y)














Method
Result
P-value




Analysis 1
Significant
0.01

Not Significant
0.15

Summarize your findings and their implications.



Add any references to papers, data sources, or resources you used.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh Using R
text:
My final project for CELL 6351 - Intro to Reproducible Data Analysis Using R.
I will analyze a maternal health risk dataset collected from hospitals and community clinics in rural Bangladesh. The dataset includes age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, heart rate, and maternal risk level. Using R and the tidyverse package, I will summarize and visualize differences among low-, mid-, and high-risk groups through bar charts, boxplots, scatterplots, and dimension-reduction methods such as PCA or UMAP. I will examine the number of patients in each risk category, differences in age, blood pressure, and blood sugar across risk groups, the clinical measurements most strongly associated with risk level, and whether PCA or UMAP can separate patients according to risk category. I will present the final analysis as a reproducible Quarto webpage containing the R code, figures, interpretations, and conclusion.
